title: The Empty Tomb and the Road to Emmaus

verses.text: On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, the women came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,
but when they entered, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
While they were puzzling over this, suddenly two men in radiant apparel stood beside them.
As the women bowed their faces to the ground in terror, the two men asked them, "Why do you look for the living among the dead?
He is not here; He has risen! Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee:
'The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.'"
Then they remembered His words.
And when they returned from the tomb, they reported all these things to the Eleven and to all the others.
It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told this to the apostles.
But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women.
Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. And after bending down and seeing only the linen cloths, he went away, wondering to himself what had happened.
That same day two of them were going to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem.
They were talking with each other about everything that had happened.
And as they talked and deliberated, Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them.
But their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.
He asked them, "What are you discussing so intently as you walk along?" They stood still, with sadness on their faces.
One of them, named Cleopas, asked Him, "Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in recent days?"
"What things?" He asked. "The events involving Jesus of Nazareth," they answered. "This man was a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people.
Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him.
But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel. And besides all this, it is the third day since these things took place.
Furthermore, some of our women astounded us. They were at the tomb early this morning,
but they did not find His body. They came and told us they had seen a vision of angels, who said that Jesus was alive.
Then some of our companions went to the tomb and found it just as the women had described. But Him they did not see."
Then Jesus said to them, "O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!
Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?"
And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.
As they approached the village where they were headed, He seemed to be going farther.
But they pleaded with Him, "Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over." So He went in to stay with them.
While He was reclining at the table with them, He took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to them.
Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus—and He disappeared from their sight.
They asked each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?"
And they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem. There they found the Eleven and those with them, gathered together
and saying, "The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!"
Then the two told what had happened on the road, and how they had recognized Jesus in the breaking of the bread.
While they were describing these events, Jesus Himself stood among them and said, "Peace be with you."
But they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit.
"Why are you troubled," Jesus asked, "and why do doubts arise in your hearts?
Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have."
And when He had said this, He showed them His hands and feet.
While they were still in disbelief because of their joy and amazement, He asked them, "Do you have anything here to eat?"
So they gave Him a piece of broiled fish,
and He took it and ate it in front of them.
Jesus said to them, "These are the words I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms."
Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
And He told them, "This is what is written: The Christ will suffer and rise from the dead on the third day,
and in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem.
You are witnesses of these things.
And behold, I am sending the promise of My Father upon you. But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high."
When Jesus had led them out as far as Bethany, He lifted up His hands and blessed them.
While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven.
And they worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
praising God continually in the temple.

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Resurrection narrative: the empty tomb, the Emmaus road, the appearance to the disciples, and the ascension
context.audience: The women, Peter, the two travelers, and the Eleven and their companions. Luke's readers are shown that the resurrection is real, bodily, and foretold in Scripture, and that they are to be witnesses.
context.mapLabel: JERUSALEM AND THE ROAD TO EMMAUS
context.setting: The chapter begins at the garden tomb outside Jerusalem, follows two travelers on a seven-mile road to Emmaus (about 11 km), and ends on the Mount of Olives near Bethany, where Jesus is carried up. The exact site of Emmaus is uncertain, and scholars have proposed several villages west and northwest of Jerusalem. Everything else happens in or near Jerusalem on the first Easter Sunday.
context.custom: Jewish tradition set the first day of the week as the day after the Sabbath, the day when the women could finally bring spices. Burial spices were to honor the body, so the women do not expect a resurrection. Sharing a meal made a guest a friend, and the way Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives the bread (v.30) echoes the feeding of the five thousand and the Last Supper.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 23 ended with the burial and the Sabbath rest. Chapter 24 is the same weekend, from the dawn of the first day to the evening, and then to the days of the ascension. Luke's second volume, Acts, begins by taking up this ending (Acts 1:1-11).
context.timelineBible: Verses 27, 44, and 46 say that Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms all point to the Christ suffering and rising, so the whole Old Testament is read as one story about Him. The promise of the Father (v.49) is the Holy Spirit, who comes at Pentecost (Acts 2). The blessing with raised hands (v.50) recalls the high priest's blessing in Leviticus 9:22.
context.sparkNotes: On the first day of the week, women find the tomb open and the body gone, and two men in dazzling clothes ask, "Why do you look for the living among the dead?" The apostles think the women's report is nonsense, though Peter runs to see for himself. That afternoon, two disciples walking to Emmaus are joined by Jesus, whom they do not recognize. He explains from Moses and all the Prophets that the Christ had to suffer and then enter His glory, and they recognize Him when He breaks bread. They hurry back to Jerusalem, where Jesus appears, shows His hands and feet, eats a piece of fish, opens their minds to understand the Scriptures, and promises power from on high. He leads them out to Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven, and they return to the temple with great joy.

translation.meaning: Literally "was raised." The passive voice points to God as the one who raised Jesus. The same word appears in the angels' announcement (v.6) and the apostles' report (v.34).
To open fully. Luke uses the same verb for the eyes opening at Emmaus (v.31), Jesus opening the Scriptures (v.32), and Jesus opening their minds (v.45). Understanding comes by Christ's opening.
Jesus read the Old Testament as a unified story pointing to Himself. Luke does not record the exact passages, which leaves readers to find them for themselves.
People who testify to what they have seen and heard. This word begins the book of Acts, where the apostles carry the message from Jerusalem to the nations.

otBackground.note: "You will not abandon me to the grave," the psalm Peter later cites for the resurrection (Acts 2:25-31).

commentary.note: Henry praises the women for coming to the tomb on the morning after the Sabbath, saying that "the zeal of some provokes others." He reads the angels' question as a rebuke to anyone who seeks Christ among dead idols, human traditions, or created things: "a reproof is given to those that look for him among the dead." On Emmaus, he notes that "their eyes were held, that they should not know him," and that Christ meets those who seek Him even before they recognize Him.

On the burning hearts, Henry says the disciples knew Jesus afterward because His teaching had moved them, and he links it to preaching that explains Scripture plainly and centers on Christ. He calls Christ "the best expositor of scripture," and says: "Christ's way of working faith in the soul, and gaining the throne there, is by opening the understanding." On the ascension, he says Jesus "did not go away in displeasure, but in love," leaving a blessing behind, and the disciples answered with worship and joy.

Gill reads the angels' question as meaning that Christ, though dead, was now alive and not to be found in a tomb, and that He is found among living saints, not "dead sinners, or lifeless professors." Of the burning hearts, he says His words carried such power that "their hearts were warmed and glowed within them." He says Jesus ate the fish not from need but to prove He had risen in a real, physical body. On verse 45, he cites the necessity of the Spirit's illumination for understanding Scripture, and on the ascension he says the parting was "only in body."

overview.summary: Women find the tomb empty, and two men in dazzling clothes say Jesus has risen. Two disciples on the road to Emmaus walk with Him without recognizing Him until He breaks bread. He appears to the eleven, opens their minds to the Scriptures, and ascends.
overview.settingLine: The tomb, the road to Emmaus, and Jerusalem.

history.t: The women came at dawn on the first day, after resting on the Sabbath.
Emmaus lay a few miles from Jerusalem, and its exact site is still debated.

customs.t: Spices honored the body, so the women did not expect a resurrection.
The host broke and blessed bread to start a meal, when they recognized Him.

archaeology.t: Rock-cut tombs of the time were sealed with rolling disk stones, as in the story.
Several places claim to be Emmaus, including Emmaus-Nicopolis and Abu Ghosh.

overview.discussion: Why might the disciples have been kept from recognizing Jesus until He broke the bread?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
